Subject: Dedicated capacity performance: streaming SLA & GPU choices

Hi Soojin,

Thanks again for the call this morning — really helpful overview. A quick recap from our side and a few clarifying questions so we can scope internal validation: 

Summary of our target workload
- Use-case: real-time clinical assistant (streaming partial tokens to UI) integrated into clinician workflow
- Model family: LLM v2-ish (~30B), autoregressive chat-style prompting, average turn ~120 tokens
- Daily throughput: ~1.2M tokens/day with cyclical peaks during morning rounds
- Concurrency target: sustained 30 concurrent sessions, burst up to 70 for ~10-15 minutes
- Latency target: 95th <= 200ms end-to-end for streamed first byte, 99th <= 350ms (we care a lot about percentiles)

Questions we need nailed for procurement and sizing
1) For streaming-first-byte SLOs above, what dedicated-reservation footprint do you recommend (GPU type + count) to hit 30 sustained / 70 burst?
2) What is expected delta between H100 and A100 for our workload (latency and tokens/sec) — we need a clear tradeoff summary for the finance team.
3) Can you run a 48-hour validation in your Dedicated environment against our sample prompt set and provide raw latency percentiles + token throughput graphs? We can ship a sanitized prompt pack and example traces.
4) Any special considerations for KV caching and concurrency when streaming partial tokens?

I've attached a short SLO worksheet so you can see how Procurement will evaluate the proposal.

Next steps we'd like: an explicit recommended config and a proposed validation plan so we can sign-off with Security & Procurement.

Thanks,

Carlos Vega
Head of Platform
NimbleHealth

Carlos — thanks for the clear recap and the SLO worksheet. Appreciate the level of detail; that helps a lot. High level answers up-front, followed by a proposed validation plan and action items.

High-level recommendation (short answer)
- Recommended baseline: 3 H100-80GB reserved GPUs for your steady-state (30 concurrent streamers).
- Burst buffer: two additional reserved instances that can be autoscaled during the 10–15 min bursts to cover up to 70 concurrent sessions.
- If budget-constrained: 4x A100-80GB is a reasonable compromise but expect ~10–18% higher 95/99th latency on streaming-first-byte and ~12% lower tokens/sec compared to H100 for models in the 20–40B class.

Why this config
- H100 gives better kernel throughput for longer contexts and streaming because of faster attention kernels and better fp8 support in our runtime.
- 3x H100 sustains your 30 concurrent streaming sessions with margin for KV cache hits (~20–25% reduction in token work) and allows background batching for non-streamed requests.

Validation plan (what we will run)
1) We’ll run a 48-hour validation in a Dedicated staging pool that mirrors your proposed network/latency envelope.
2) Tests we will execute:
   - Baseline single-session latency profiling (cold vs warm KV cache)
   - Concurrency sweep: 5, 15, 30, 50, 70 sessions with realistic interleaving
   - Burst simulation (70 concurrent for 15m window, repeat x3)
   - Streaming-first-byte and full-response streaming percentiles (p50/p95/p99)
   - Tokens/sec throughput and GPU utilization traces
3) Deliverables:
   - Raw histogram outputs (p50/p90/p95/p99), token throughput over time, kernel-level GPU metrics (utilization, memory, power)
   - Comparison H100 vs A100 run (same model/checkpoint, same prompt pack)

What we need from you
- Sanitized prompt pack (you mentioned that will be ready tomorrow)
- Target SLA language (we’ll map our observed p99 numbers to a proposed contract SLA)
- A short list of three example sessions that are highest priority for UX (we’ll instrument those more finely)

Timeline
- Validation kickoff: As soon as we have the prompt pack (target: Nov 19).
- Internal run + analysis: 48 hours running + 48 hours analysis = deliverable by Nov 24.

Attachments: I’m attaching our preliminary GPU matrix and the Dedicated playbook to show the assumptions we use (batching, cache ttl, kernel flags).

Next meeting
- Can we do a 30-minute technical sync early next week after you confirm the prompt pack? I’ll have Aditya join for the load tooling discussion.

Regards,

Soojin Lee

Hi all — quick tech note on the validation so Carlos & Lucia know exactly what we’ll measure and how to interpret results.

Test harness and metrics
- We will use our load runner with the streaming proxy that mirrors client-side keepalive and chunk sizes. The harness will emit per-request: first_byte_latency_ms, last_byte_latency_ms, tokens_generated, gpu_util_pct, mem_bytes_used.
- We’ll collect kernel-level traces for a representative subset of requests to measure attention kernel latencies and kv cache hit rates.

H100 vs A100 matrix (summary)
- H100-80GB: ~+10–18% tokens/sec vs A100 for 20–40B autoregressive models (measured on our runtime internal benchmarks). Better p99 stability under high concurrency because of fp8 kernel throughput.
- A100-80GB: cheaper per-hour. Expect slightly higher latency tail when streaming many small partial tokens.
- L4 / cheaper L-class options: not recommended for sustained streaming concurrency >20 because of lower memory bandwidth and smaller cache sizes.

Sizing rule-of-thumb we’ll validate
- Steady-concurrency 1 GPU handles ~12–15 concurrent streaming sessions for your model at p95 <= 200ms (H100). So 3xH100 maps to ~36–45 concurrent sustain with margin.
- For bursts, autoscale using reserved + burst pool (we recommend 2 additional reserved units) — that gives capacity headroom without cold-starts.

Data we need from your side
- Prompt pack (sanitized)
- A realistic concurrency profile (CSV) with timestamps for a 24–48h period if you have it (helps us tune burst cadence).

Deliverables (technical)
- Per-GPU run artifacts (JSON lines) with sampled request traces
- A summary CSV for latency percentiles by concurrency point
- Short recommendations section: whether H100 is justified vs A100 for the observed economics

I’ll upload the test harness and a small example load script to the Drive link in Soojin’s note.
